vignette:
He is sitting at the kitchen table, morning coffee gone cold, when the scent of diesel from the neighbor’s lawnmower drifts through the window. His shoulders lock. His breathing turns shallow. He sees the greenish-yellow plume again, rolling across the water, and in his nostrils the acrid burn of toluene and xylene. That was forty-three years ago.

It happened in the Gulf of Guinea, during a routine inspection of a disabled tanker. He was a senior petty officer in the Coast Guard, responsible for the boarding team. The containment valve had cracked, and a cloud of petrochemical vapor spewed upward. No one had warned them. Within seconds the air was thick, eyes stinging, throats closing. He remembers shouting for everyone to get back, remembers the metallic taste, the panic in the young seaman’s voice. They were evacuated, but not before he had taken three deep breaths—each one a debt he is still paying.

The burns on his lungs healed, or seemed to. He retired early with a medical pension. But the debt was never chemical alone. In the months and years that followed, he began to avoid the sea. He told his wife it was arthritis, told his children he preferred the garden. But the garden smelled like damp earth, not salt, and he would not step onto a boat even for a family outing. He stopped watching the news. If a ship horn sounded on the television, he would freeze, remote in hand, until the sound passed.

Now, at seventy-two, he lives in a quiet suburb far from any coast. His wife has learned to keep the windows closed during spring when farmers spray their fields. She buys unscented detergent, because lavender reminds him of the decontamination showers. She does not complain when he wakes at three in the morning, thrashing, drenched in sweat, muttering about the valve. He never tells her what he dreams: the young seaman’s face, the way the chemical fog swallowed the deck, the moment he thought he would die.

He has not touched a gas can in twenty years. He drives an electric car. He walks the long way around a neighbor’s house if they are painting. At the hardware store, the aisle with cleaning solvents makes him dizzy—a kind of vertigo that feels like falling. He avoids crowds, avoids any gathering where people might wear respirators (he once walked out of a hospital waiting room when he saw a nurse with an N95 mask). He tells himself he is prudent. He knows he is afraid.

His wife asks him to go for a walk on the beach. He says no. She asks why. He says the sand reminds him of something. She does not press. She knows the something.

Last week, a truck backfired on their street. He dropped to the ground, cover his head, and stayed there for a full minute, trembling, while the mailman stared. His wife helped him up. She did not scold. She just held his hand. But he saw the worry in her eyes, the same worry he sees every morning when he checks the weather—checking the wind direction out of habit, scanning the horizon for a plume that is not there.

He knows the world is not the Gulf of Guinea. He knows no tankers sail through his living room. And yet, when the scent of diesel rises, his body remembers before his mind can reason. He sits at the table, coffee cold, and waits for the panic to pass. It always does. But it always comes back.
